Hamor
hā´mōr
n. pr. m. (Hebrew Chamor, an ass; prince of Shechem)
Hebrew chamor, a he-ass — a beast of burden and of peace rather than of war. He was the Hivite prince from whose sons Jacob bought his field.

Biblical Definition

Hamor is the Hivite prince of Shechem, and his name marks both a purchase and a massacre. Jacob dealt honestly with his house: “And he bought a parcel of a field, where he had spread his tent, at the hand of the children of Hamor, Shechem's father, for an hundred pieces of money” (Gen 33:19) — the ground where Joseph's bones were finally buried. Then his son destroyed the peace: “And when Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of the country, saw her, he took her, and lay with her, and defiled her” (Gen 34:2). Hamor came to negotiate: “And Hamor the father of Shechem went out unto Jacob to commune with him” (Gen 34:6), and pleaded his son's case: “The soul of my son Shechem longeth for your daughter: I pray you give her him to wife” (Gen 34:8). Jacob's sons answered deceitfully, required circumcision of every male, and on the third day Simeon and Levi slew them all. Hamor and Shechem died in the city Hamor had ruled, and Jacob's deathbed word on it is not admiration but a curse upon their anger.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) does not treat Scripture proper names; the sense is Hebrew, chamor, an ass — the common beast of burden in Canaan.

HAMOR. A Hebrew proper name; chamor, an ass.

PRINCE, n. In a general sense, a sovereign; the chief and independent ruler of a nation or state.

COMMUNE, v.i. To converse; to talk together familiarly; to impart sentiments mutually.

Key Scripture

Gen 33:19 — "And he bought a parcel of a field, where he had spread his tent, at the hand of the children of Hamor, Shechem's father, for an hundred pieces of money."

Gen 34:2 — "And when Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of the country, saw her, he took her, and lay with her, and defiled her."

Gen 34:6 — "And Hamor the father of Shechem went out unto Jacob to commune with him."

Gen 34:8 — "And Hamor communed with them, saying, The soul of my son Shechem longeth for your daughter: I pray you give her him to wife."

Modern Corruption

Genesis 34 is read as either a defence of vengeance or an indictment of Scripture, when the narrative condemns the assault and the massacre alike.

expand to see more

Genesis 34 records a rape and a slaughter and endorses neither. Shechem's act is called folly in Israel, a thing which ought not to be done, and the narrative gives Dinah's brothers a real grievance. But Jacob's verdict on Simeon and Levi, delivered on his deathbed and therefore with the weight of a patriarchal oracle, is unsparing: cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel. Scripture's habit of reporting what its heroes did without approving it is the very thing that makes it trustworthy history rather than propaganda.

Hamor himself is the study in expedient fatherhood. His son had committed an atrocity, and the prince came to negotiate a marriage and a trade agreement — make ye marriages with us, and the land shall be before you. Not a word of rebuke to Shechem is recorded. A father who treats his son's grave sin as a diplomatic problem to be managed has already handed him over, and both of them died for it in the gate of their own city.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Chamor (H2544), Hamor; from chamor (H2543), an ass; the Hivites (H2340) were among the nations of Canaan.

expand to see more

Hebrew Chamor (H2544) — Hamor; Genesis 33:19, 34:2, 34:6.

Hebrew chamor (H2543) — an ass; the common noun behind the name.

Hebrew Chivvi (H2340) — Hivite; one of the seven nations of Canaan.

Hebrew nebalah (H5039) — folly, disgraceful act; the term Genesis 34:7 uses of Shechem's deed.

Hebrew Shekem (H7927) — Shechem; both the son and the city.

Usage

"“He bought a parcel of a field… at the hand of the children of Hamor” — and Joseph was buried in it."

"“Hamor the father of Shechem went out unto Jacob to commune with him” — to negotiate, not to rebuke."

"“The soul of my son Shechem longeth for your daughter” — a father's plea after an atrocity."
